questions.text: For a given biased coin, the probability that the outcome of a toss is a head is 0.4. This coin is tossed 1,000 times. Let X denote the random variable whose value is the number of times that head appeared in these 1,000 tosses. The standard deviation of X (rounded to 2 decimal place) is ________
questions.solution:
X is binomial with n = 1000, p = 0.4.
[latex]\sigma=\sqrt{np(1-p)}=\sqrt{1000\times0.4\times0.6}=\sqrt{240}\approx15.49[/latex]

Answer: 15.49

questions.text:
Choose the correct choice(s) regarding the following proportional logic assertion S:

[latex]S: (( P \wedge Q) \rightarrow R) \rightarrow (( P \wedge Q) \rightarrow (Q \rightarrow R))[/latex]
questions.solution:
Simplify the consequent: [latex](P\wedge Q)\rightarrow(Q\rightarrow R)\equiv(P\wedge Q\wedge Q)\rightarrow R\equiv(P\wedge Q)\rightarrow R[/latex], which is exactly the antecedent.

So S has the form [latex]A\rightarrow A[/latex], which is always true.

Answer: S is a tautology; its antecedent is equivalent to its consequent

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: S  is neither a tautology nor a contradiction
The antecedent of S is logically equivalent to the consequent of S

questions.text:
Consider the following sets, where [latex]n\geq 2[/latex]:

S1: Set of all nxn matrices with entries from the set [latex]\{a, b, c\}[/latex]
S2: Set of all functions from the set[latex]\{0,1,2,...,n^2-1\}[/latex] to the set [latex]\{0, 1, 2 \}[/latex]

Which of the following choice(s) is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]|S_1|=3^{n^2}[/latex] (each of the [latex]n^2[/latex] entries has 3 choices).
- [latex]|S_2|=3^{n^2}[/latex] (each of the [latex]n^2[/latex] inputs has 3 choices).

Equal finite sizes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] a bijection exists (read the matrix entries in order as the function values). A bijection is also a surjection and an injection.

Answer: A surjection exists; a bijection exists

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: There does not exist a bijection from S1 to S2
There exists a surjection from S1 to S2
There exists a bijection from S1 to S2
There does not exist an injection from S1 to S2

questions.text:
A sender (S) transmits a signal, which can be one of the two kinds: H and L with probabilities 0.1 and 0.9 respectively, to a receiver (R)
In the graph below, the weight of edge [latex](u,v)[/latex] is the probability of receiving [latex]v[/latex] when [latex]u[/latex] is transmitted, where [latex]u,v\in\{H,L\}[/latex]. For example, the probability that the received signal is [latex]L[/latex] given the transmitted signal was [latex]H[/latex], is 0.7.

If the received signal is [latex]H[/latex], the probability that the transmitted signal was [latex]H[/latex] (rounded to 2 decimal places) is __________.
questions.solution:
From the graph: P(recv H | sent H) = 0.3 and P(recv H | sent L) = 0.8.

P(recv H) = 0.1 [latex]\times[/latex] 0.3 + 0.9 [latex]\times[/latex] 0.8 = 0.03 + 0.72 = 0.75

Bayes: [latex]P(\text{sent H}\mid\text{recv H})=\frac{0.03}{0.75}=0.04[/latex]

Answer: 0.04

questions.text:
A relation [latex]R[/latex] is said to be circular if [latex]aRb[/latex] and [latex]bRc[/latex] together imply [latex]cRa[/latex].
Which of the following options is/are correct?
questions.solution:
Reflexive + circular gives an equivalence relation:
- Symmetric: aRb and bRb (reflexive) [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] bRa (circular).
- Transitive: aRb and bRc [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] cRa (circular) [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] aRc (symmetric).

The others fail: reflexive + symmetric need not be transitive; circular + symmetric need not be reflexive (e.g. the empty relation); transitive + circular need not be reflexive either.

Answer: Reflexive and circular [latex]\Rightarrow[/latex] equivalence relation

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: If a relation S is reflexive and symmetric, then S is an equivalence relation.
If a relation S is circular and symmetric, then S is an equivalence relation.
If a relation S is reflexive and circular, then S is an equivalence relation.
If a relation S is transitive and circular, then S is an equivalence relation.
